job.theme: the life of a famous Indian scientist
job.style: a comparison of two related ideas

response.passage: Sir C.V. Raman was a man of deep curiosity, often comparing the blue of the Mediterranean Sea to the vast Indian Ocean. In 1921, while traveling on a ship, he observed the deep blue hue of the water and wondered if it was merely a reflection of the sky. He later discovered that the blue color is caused by the scattering of sunlight by water molecules. This phenomenon, now known as the Raman Effect, earned him the Nobel Prize in 1930. While many believed the color came from the sky, Raman proved that the water itself scatters light. He often worked alongside his colleague K.S. Krishnan at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Kolkata. Raman was a strict disciplinarian, once famously stating that science requires a spirit of inquiry rather than just following textbooks. He spent his later years in Bengaluru, where he established the Raman Research Institute. His work remains a pillar of modern physics, proving that even simple observations can lead to groundbreaking discoveries. Unlike the static nature of laboratory experiments, Raman believed that nature itself was the greatest laboratory for a scientist to explore.
response.summary: Sir C.V. Raman discovered that the blue color of the ocean is caused by light scattering rather than sky reflection. His work on this phenomenon earned him international recognition and led to the founding of a research institute in Bengaluru.
